O que muda no trabalho de social media com os novos dados do Google Search Console? Spoilier: muda tudo. Rosto sorridente rachado, picles e farol: conheça os novos emojis do iPhone 2027. Eu amo. Cada novo emoji abre novas possibilidades de comunicação pra gente. Essa semana rolou um bafafá sobre a fonte anti-IA, que só os humanos conseguem ler . Mas já foi testado e comprovado que as IAs conseguem ler, sim. Leia a thread abaixo do comentário do usuário SeriouslyYoutube. Autoridades britânicas propõem o apagão das redes sociais para adolescentes durante a noite. União Europeia exige que Meta mude o ‘design viciante’ do Facebook e do Instagram e é importante a gente acompanhar o caso. 🧠 Estão questionando diretamente o modelo que sustenta as principais métricas das redes sociais. Influenciadores viraram fonte de informação sobre saúde. Pew analisa como jovens consomem conteúdo de saúde . Perigoso demais, vixe. Alô Mari Kruguer! Ela já já participa da consideração, mas ainda não conquistou confiança suficiente para assumir a decisão. BCG mede a influência da IA sobre as decisões. O número de pessoas que usa a ferramenta pra pesquisas marcas e serviços segue crescendo. 🧠 O marketing passa a trabalhar com dois caminhos de influência: um voltado à atenção humana e outro à avaliação feita por sistemas. trabalho cada vez mais complexo, e cada vez menos amador Artigo: Evite que a IA prejudique sua marc a . Harvard Business Review alerta para o desgaste acumulado pela automação Dados próprios aumentam as chances de citação pela IA. A Similarweb defende que levantamentos, pesquisas e números exclusivos dão aos sistemas de IA um motivo concreto para citar a fonte original. 🧠 Dados internos podem virar conteúdo de autoridade. Mas precisam ser publicados com número, metodologia, amostra, período e fonte claramente visíveis, e não enterrados em um PDF impossível de encontrar. MANDA DICAS Hootsuite atualiza guia de mensuração de ROI nas redes sociais. Sprout Social ensina a avaliar se vale entrar no Bluesky e como criar estratégias pra lá. Estratégia de marketing com micro-influenciadore s: como encontrar, fazer parceria e medir pequenos criadores, via Later. Como as principais marcas estão ativando criadores no TikTok para impulsionar resultados reais de negócios, via Later. Agora, as novidades de cada rede. INSTAGRAM Adam Mosseri diz que creators humanos ficarão mais valiosos com a enxurrada de IA. Ele argumentou que, quanto mais conteúdo sintético circular, maior será o valor de perspectivas humanas. Instagram prepara cobrança pelo uso de I A. Mosseri confirmou que futuras ferramentas de IA do Instagram deverão ter limites de uso gratuito e opções pagas. Instagram Reels adiciona mais traduções de IA em japonês, coreano, francês, alemão e italiano Instagram começa a alertar responsáveis sobre conversas preocupantes com a Meta AI FACEBOOK/META Recuou : Dois dias depois de liberar um recurso que permitia citar contas públicas do Instagram e usar seus conteúdos em imagens geradas por IA, a Meta tirou a função do ar. Meta adiciona novas métricas para acompanhar o desempenho dos chatbots THREADS O Threads agora permite curtidas privadas , onde apenas você e a pessoa que postou poderão ver que você curtiu a postagem dela. Threads adiciona tags para posts da comunidade TELEGRAM Adorei! O Telegram lançou um e ditor para textos com até 32.768 caracteres , títulos, tabelas, listas, imagens e vídeos incorporados. A atualização também permite reunir diferentes canais, grupos e bots dentro de uma mesma Comunidade. Empresa vai testar sistemas para identificar contas dedicadas a publicar grandes volumes de conteúdo gerado por IA, e lança medidas de alfabetização . Algumas marcas já começaram a proibir esse tipo de conteúdo. Vendedores do TikTok Shop no Reino Unido ganharam um painel mais detalhado para entender como os produtos são descobertos. 🧠 Estar por dentro dos lançamentos das ferramentas é importante, mesmo quando não estão liberadas por aqui ainda. É uma forma de se preparar para as novidades que estão chegando. A proposta é aumentar a presença de relações reais e reduzir interações excessivamente hostis entre desconhecidos. Que evolução! X alterou também seu sistema para de tectar contas adeptas do engagement bait . Isso é interessante: X transforma prova social em anúncio . Usuários poderão realizar ações em aplicativos como Canva, Instacart e YouTube Music sem sair da experiência de busca. Quando as marcas usam ferramentas de inteligência artificial generativa em suas promoções, o SynthID do Google detectará e rotulará automaticamente o conteúdo. NOS VEMOS PESSOALMENTE? title: Out There
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for October is WATER. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . Check it out! “Writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Fall (or at least post-summer) finally seems to be arriving here in New Orleans. And it is almost time — wherever you are — for Write Out . This is an annual undertaking of the National Writing Project , developed in conjunction with the National Park Service . As I wrote last year : The core idea is pretty simple: get outside, and write. Write about your environment, write to your environment, observe and attend to nature, use the craft of writing to sharpen your senses, and use your senses to sharpen your writing. “The goal is to be inspired by the world around us ,” the NWP writes, “and to connect and learn through place-based writing and sharing.” Nothing (well, maybe apart from the actual weather) is stopping you from writing outside any time. But Write Out is a kick in the pants, a kind of open-to-anyone annual two-week event, which the NWP promotes through various prompts and other resources aimed at educators but available to all. This year Write Out happens October 11–25, with the lovely theme Write Where We Stand — “writing in the places that shape and sustain us.” Every year NWP publishes a “ choice board ” of theme-related prompts; here are a few (condensed and slightly modified versions) of my favorites for this year. (Click through on each prompt title for the full NWP context/instructions.) Poetically Advocate A Place You Love . Take inspiration from Don Welch’s poem “ Advice From a Provincial ,“ and identify three “outdoor images or phenomena that are wondrous about your place. Use them to create a poetic letter to someone who doesn’t really know” the place you love, or at least not like you know it. Link Words and Image s. Snap some pictures around your community. Take your time. Choose one that captures something to celebrate — and one that captures something you would like to change. Pair these images. “ What story do they tell when you look at them together? Give your story a title, caption your images, and share your work.” Speak Like A River. Poets Amanda Eke and Mario José Pagán Morales consider the Bronx River, and what stories it might tell. In a place you know, reflect on “ what that place has witnessed , remembered, celebrated, protected, or survived. … If this river, tree, park, or wooded pathway could talk — tell us poems, tell us stories — what do you think it would say?” Write about it. Leave a comment THERE’S MORE! In connection with Write Out, there are two online events that sound cool: Hawaiian Kilo: Writing Rooted in Place Native Hawaiians developed a practice known as Kilo — “to watch, observe, examine, or forecast.” This means closely observing the natural world and its patterns, ideally to better steward the environment. A Zoom workshop, “led by teachers from the Waiākea Intermediate School in Hilo Hawai'i,” happens October 13, 2026, 6 pm US Central time . Details and (free) registration here . Haiku + Comic = Haikomic The Write Time with Write Out Ambassador Grant Snider on October 20 . Snider is a writer/artist who combines haiku with comics. (Details on that here , and at his newsletter. ) And he is this year’s Write Out Author Ambassador. Check the Write Out newsletter for event details as they emerge. I really like the sound of this and hope to revisit. Grant Snider, via Incidental Comics Leave a comment PS I was a Write Out Ambassador last year. I love Write Out! Mark Frauenfelder found one in English called The Blind Man , co-edited by Marcel Duchamp. Its second issue, from 1917, covered the controversy around Duchamp’s Fountain , a urinal he submitted under the name Richard Mutt to the Society of Independent Artists exhibition. description: nas edições anteriores #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 A essa altura você já sabe que a Bits to Brands virou uma revista impressa . Duas, na verdade, considerando que estamos na segunda edição. Já somos praticamente uma banca. O que você talvez não saiba é que este processo criativo começou lá em 2014, quando a gente visualizou uma revista impressa que viria com um boné, feita para ser a companhia ideal para o verão de 2025. (Por isso a garota da capa estava sentada em uma cadeira de praia lendo uma revista, que dentro tinha uma página só de palavras cruzadas e vinha com um cartão postal retratando um dia de praia…) Ou seja: não basta selecionar os artigos, ordenar e diagramar de forma que faça sentido e pensar o projeto gráfico - toda revista precisa ter um tema. _ Na sua segunda edição, em 2026, o escolhido foi Bora de Brasil . Uma das grandes tendências do ano, e um tema de grande interesse por aqui - das pesquisas traduzindo a nossa cultura à possibilidade de contar mais histórias de marcas brasileiras. Imagina não ser brasileiro e não reparar no rodinho de pia? A celebração da brasilidade foi o norte para a capa, o título, as cores, a curadoria de artigos e, claro, para a experiência memorável que a gente quer que a revista seja. Aqui a gente não coloca impresso no mundo para ir parar no fundo da gaveta. Ou é para guardar, ou é para expor, ou é para interagir. Ou quem sabe até todas as anteriores. É por isso que, dessa vez, ela tem uma lombada quadrada (fica melhor na estante) , tem uma página que vira pôster (um lembrete para a sua área de trabalho) e tem um álbum de figurinhas. _ Brasilidade + impresso + offline + Copa do Mundo. A cada quatro anos essas referências se encontram na sensação de completar, uma de cada vez, dezenas de páginas de um álbum. As figurinhas, por sua vez, trazem imagens conhecidas, reconhecidas, algumas até icônicas, que representam o melhor do país naquela modalidade. A nossa modalidade é o marketing. A nossa seleção, portanto, é composta de ações de marcas que destacam o melhor da criatividade brasileira nas últimas décadas. Fiquem agora com a nossa Seleção, na certeza de que ela deixou grandes destaques de fora. Porém com a esperança de que isso gere bons debates e trocas. _ Em 2013, a Kombi contava em primeira pessoa as histórias reais que as pessoas enviaram para celebrar a sua despedida. Em 1998, a Johnson’s Baby reforçava a sua linha de shampoos infantis, e oferecia a trilha sonora para milhões de banhos de bebês dali em diante. Em 2019, o McDonald’s deixava de lado a consistência em nome do seu real significado (e grafia) para o público brasileiro. Em 1997, dois pequenos esquimós transformavam Danoninho em sorvetinho, e a gente ganhava uma frase para repetir por décadas. Em 2025, a Red Bull transformava um edifício icônico de Porto Alegre em rampa para um dos maiores skatistas do Brasil. Em 2011, alguns pôneis cantavam em volta de um carro Nissan , em um dos virais mais marcantes do início das redes sociais. Em 2020, a Netflix esgotava em algumas horas uma edição especial impressa do seu universo de conteúdo. Em 1991, uma série de conteúdos transformava uma marca em adjetivo e fazia muita gente se questionar se qualquer coisa era ou não era “assim uma Brastemp ”... Em 2025, o Canva colocou a Xuxa em um dos seus figurinos icônicos para lançar uma linha de produtos e uma campanha especial “para adultinhos”. _ Além de uma Seleção de Campanhas, a Revista Bits to Brands tem 50 páginas de conteúdo e ilustrações. Ela é a materialização da nossa identidade visual e conteúdo, e também daquilo que a gente acredita: o poder das palavras, a conexão para além das telas e o valor que as coisas ganham quando passam a fazer parte da vida real de alguém. Para viabilizar o seu envio para diferentes cantos do Brasil, estamos fazendo uma tiragem especial em forma de produto social. Você pode garantir a sua pelo valor de R$ 79,90 - e todo o lucro desta ação será destinado a uma ONG de incentivo à leitura no Brasil. Esperamos que seja uma boa leitura, uma ótima surpresa e algo significativo e duradouro como só o impresso é capaz de se tornar. Sem mais delongas: EU QUERO UMA REVISTA (é só clicar no botão - enquanto durar o estoque) para inspirar, com O Boticário #publi ✨ A nova linha Nativa SPA Ameixa Intensa foi anunciada com uma mescla de conteúdo orgânico, influenciadores e até ameixas gigantes. E O Boticário mostrou que uma boa estratégia de comunicação acontece entre o online e o offline, agregando ao entretenimento ao invés de interrompê-lo. Durante a novela Quem Ama Cuida, a marca foi inserida em meio a dois personagens que representam o seu principal atributo: intensidade. Na cena, amostras do novo hidratante são usadas e mencionadas de forma sutil. Só no break comercial que a mensagem se completa: dobro de ameixa, dobro de amostras nas lojas. E o link com oferta vai para as redes sociais minutos depois. description: nas edições anteriores #300 | A vida das coisas #301 | O legado da Copa do Mundo 2026 tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 do dicionário: oráculo, substantivo masculino Num lugar sagrado, resposta a uma pergunta feita a uma divindade cujo teor era entendido como profético, sendo de difícil compreensão, obscuro. Resposta dada por uma divindade, quando alguém a consultava. Pessoa que, supostamente, prevê o futuro ou a previsão feita por essa pessoa. _ Nada contra carrosseis de Instagram. Inclusive, fazemos vários. O formato inicialmente permitia compartilhar dez imagens em um único post, e depois foi expandido para vinte. Primeiro, foi utilizado pelos millennials como álbum do Orkut - registros agrupados de um mesmo evento. Depois a gen Z, querendo performar menos, intercalou fotos posadas com fotos aleatórias e chamou de dump . Enquanto isso, a bolha criadora de conteúdo tratava as telas como slides e elaborava apresentações sobre todo tipo de assunto - com call to action no final, claro. Salve, compartilhe, assine, contrate, inscreva-se. O carrossel é um dos formatos preferidos de quem busca engajamento. Basta um questionamento bem amplo e chamativo na capa, seguido por uma série de telas que ora explicam, ora confundem. O resultado é a banalização de questões extremamente profundas - como se a resposta coubesse em um carrossel de Instagram. Ou como se eles fossem de fato lidos com a devida atenção, ou escritos com a pretensão de elaborar uma pauta para além do rage bait da capa. Como se eles fossem sequer escritos por uma outra pessoa. _ Nada contra carrosseis de Instagram. Inclusive, fazemos vários. É muito útil poder intercalar explicações com imagens, organizar textos de forma compartilhável, ampliar discussões e aumentar a audiência sem depender de vídeos curtos. A inteligência artificial é uma grande aliada nesta organização de informações e layout para expressar ideias. Agora, a disseminação dos carrosseis feitos por inteligência artificial, posicionando suas fontes como oráculos contemporâneos das gerações, do brasileiro ou de qualquer tipo de comportamento tem servido mais para vender, do que para informar. No grande mercado que virou a timeline, a atual recomendação é juntar o questionamento profundo com a elaboração rasa e o call to action certo no final. Assim, vamos arrastando para cima de uma pergunta para outra e delegando a nossa capacidade de reflexão ao marketing digital. De repente, parece que questões complexas cabem nesse tipo de generalização, que gerações inteiras podem ser reduzidas a frases de efeito, ou que estratégias elaboradas podem ser decifradas em algumas telas. _ Perguntas são feitas desde que o mundo é mundo. And after a while, that kind of noise starts to play gams with the old brain. But, a lot of this noise is lazy thinking at best, because there is no future creative industry without creative people. And a world without creatives is not a world I, or anyone I speak to, wants to see. So… instead of just talking about it, I’ve teamed up with my awesome pals at Affinity to actually do something about it. The program is f-r-e-e. Properly free. Not watered-down, stripped-back, “you get half the experience” kind of free… it’s the real fucking deal. It doesn’t matter where you’re based, what creative discipline you’re part of, what software you use, or where you’re at with your skillset. We’re all about backing people who are willing to show up and take action. Each cohort of the Super Duper Mentorship will have 100 creatives in it. If you don’t get in the first time, there’ll be another intake, and another after that. We’ll keep this going every year, for as long as people have the energy to show up and participate. If you’re a designer, artist, illustrator, photographer, or just a generally creative human wanting to make cool shit… this has been built for you. Key Dates: Applications Open: today, 30th June 2026 Applications close: 14th July 2026 (you’ll hear back from us by the 24th of July) Doors open for Cohort 1: Monday 3rd August 2026 Weekly calls: Tuesdays, 6pm BST The Mentorship will run online inside the private Super Duper Circle community, hosted by myself and some very special guest appearances. APPLY HERE What the Mentorship Covers: The program runs in two phases. Phase One: Reframing and Rethinking The first 90 days, we’ll focus on mindset, clarity, and direction. You’ll work through the habits, assumptions, and overthinking patterns that often hold creatives back. You’ll explore: creative positioning pricing and boundaries reputation and trust building an offer around your skills We’ll help you move from confusion and hesitation to confidence and clarity. Phase Two: Action and Application The final 30 days of the mentorship are where things get practical. We are going to build something real together: We will create some cool artwork Pop it onto some cool product Send you the items for freebies You can sell them to make some monies. Everything in the Super Duper Mentorship is practical and built around participation. You’re not just taking in advice, you’re applying it and taking action. Testing ideas, getting feedback, and refining as you go. By the end of our four months together, you’ll go from being good at your craft to becoming a more employable and entrepreneurial creative who can build opportunities around your skills, have real (and meaningful) conversations with real people, and turn your ideas into something that actually works in the real world. Let’s fucking go. And if you know someone who’s early on in their creative journey, send this their way. A friend, a son or daughter, a colleague… anyone who needs a bit of direction and a proper shot. I need your help to get this in front of the right people. title: The Industry Swap Experiment
description: An amazingly random thing happened this last week. I found myself in Moab, Utah, with around 70 total strangers who now feel like my best friends. I was invited by my buddy Jason to speak at the first-ever Summer Camp hosted by his company, Rupt, for the promotional products industry. There were team colours, a healthy dose of friendly competition, prizes, adventures and learning sessions, all set against the incredible backdrop of the Colorado River and the red rock desert. It was fucking Magical. As a brand guy I often find myself around brand people whether thats agency owners, designers or people building things in the creative space but I have always loved to pop myself in the deep water of the unknowing. I know very little about this world. Like most people, I’ve interacted with the industry countless times as an end user. Whether that’s branded merch, company swag, event giveaways or promotional products arriving in the post… but I’ve never actually spent too much time inside the industry itself or with the people who make it all happen… so on paper, I had absolutely no business being there. But that’s exactly why I jumped at the chance to speak at this event. I love learning new things, and this room was packed with some of the biggest hitters in the game. People who have spent years building businesses and solving problems in a world I know jack shit about. It would have been easy to say no. The travel was long, the industry was unfamiliar but saying no to this opportunity was never really on the cards for me. I am getting older, and as that happens, the more I think one of the biggest mistakes we make is only learning from people who do the same thing as us. We all read the same design books, follow pretty much the same people, attend the same conferences and end up having the same conversations over and over again. This felt like the exact opposite of that… I’m gonna call it the ‘anti-echo chamber’ move. An opportunity to step outside my own little corner of the world and spend time with people who think differently and see things through a completely different lens. I had a feeling it would open my brain up in ways it hadn’t been before, and it absolutely did. Now, even though this space doesn’t live and breathe design in the same way mine does, it still lives in the world of branding. Most brand people spend their time on the fun stuff like the thinking, story, and execution side of design. We help make strategic decisions, build the identity, and create the funky punky assets. Then, more often than not, we release the work into the wild and hope it finds its way. What really hit home for me whilst spending time with this incredible group of humans is that this industry is actually much closer to mine than I first realised. They’re positioned at an incredibly important point in the journey… where the identity of a company meets real humans in the real world. They are a key part of what we do because they help bring businesses to life through experiences. And ultimately, that’s where ‘brand status’ is earned. As brand people, we’re in the game of pattern building and memory. We help businesses become recognisable. The promotional products industry helps those companies show up in the real world, creating physical touch-points and experiences that reinforce everything the business is trying to stand for. The biggest takeaway for me this week, apart from the fact that Moab might be one of the coolest places on the planet, is that every industry has its own wisdom. Every industry has people solving interesting problems and has a lot of knowledge to offer the general outsider who is keen to learn a new perspective. It’s easy to convince ourselves that all the answers live inside our own little bubble, but I’ve found over the years that many of the best ideas and implementations in my own business have come from looking outside of design. Whether that’s borrowing hospitality thinking and applying it to my design process, or building an identity of my own that fuses tattoo culture with skate-shop vibes, the things that have helped me stand out have not come from simply doing what everyone else was doing. One of the ideas I shared during my talk was Hotelling’s Law … the observation that competitors naturally drift towards sameness because it feels safer. Over time, everyone starts looking similar, sounding similar and offering similar things because nobody wants to stray too far from what appears to be working for others. The irony though is that the safest thing to do often becomes the riskiest thing to do. If everybody moves towards the middle, the middle becomes really freaking crowded. Which is why I’ve always been more interested in pushing at the edges… That’s where the interesting opportunities live. That’s why I think we should all spend a little more time making anti-echo chamber moves. Here are some ways you can do that: 1. Go to the event that isn’t built for you. 2. Read the book that nobody in your industry is talking about. 3. Spend time with people who challenge your assumptions. 4. Put yourself in rooms where you’re not the expert. Remember, my friends… curiosity is often where the magic lives. And if my week in the Utah desert taught me anything, it’s that sometimes the most valuable thing you can do isn’t go deeper into your own world… It’s to spend some time exploring somebody else’s. Big love and respect. James - The People’s Branding Mentor

title: The Unscriptable Moments That Build Reputation
description: Hello my champions of creative goodness. How are ya? Today I want to dive into a little topic that I am super passionate about, and that is the human goodness we can do to elevate the experience for the people we work with. Everyone reading this is a craft-based, creativity-infused builder of things. You might own a business, work with brands, or create cool visuals for people who love looking at cool visuals. I don’t think creative people like that need motivation to continue doing the things they already do so well, but I do think there is another layer we often forget to think about… the human layer. The stuff on top of the craft. That is where some new magic can be found. It looks like over the coming years a lot of businesses and brands will automate huge parts of their customer journey, which is logical, so the question for me becomes… Where does the human come in and make a decision that was not obvious? I am all for becoming more efficient and dialling in a good process, as many of you will know, but it’s often the stupid-on-paper, “not good for business” decisions that build a reputation worth talking about. One of my favourite examples of human creativity elevating a brand’s reputation is the story of Joshie the Giraffe. A family went on holiday to California and accidentally left their son’s stuffed giraffe at a Ritz-Carlton hotel where they were staying. To put the little boy at ease, his dad told a little white lie and said Joshie had decided to stay behind for an extra holiday. The dad had phoned the hotel and asked if they could find it, send it back, and hopefully reunite the little guy with his giraffe. The hotel staff found Joshie amongst the laundry and could have simply posted the toy back. But instead, they created an entire photo album showing Joshie relaxing by the pool, driving golf carts, getting spa treatments with cucumbers over his eyes, and “enjoying his extended vacation” before finally sending him home, all to back up his dad’s story. That tiny, unscriptable moment of human creativity transformed a forgotten toy into a story that millions of people still talk about today… just like I am right now. And I think that’s freaking fascinating. Because I doubt that family remembers much about the facilities at the Ritz-Carlton, the weather, or even how good the food was… but they will absolutely remember Joshie’s holiday forever. This got the old curiosity up… Why do moments like this stick with us so deeply while so many other experiences disappear from memory almost immediately? Why do we instantly want to tell our mates about them, repost them online and emotionally connect with complete strangers because of them? For that we probably need to get a little ‘sciencey’. Now remember, I’m not a scientist. I’m just an inquisitive bloke with a scraggly beard who spends far too much time researching human behaviour, but here’s what I found out… Your brain is basically a very clever prediction machine. Most of the time, your brain is trying to conserve energy by guessing what is about to happen next based on previous experiences and familiar patterns. If things go exactly as expected, the brain doesn’t need to pay much attention because nothing new or important is happening. Win for brain power. This is why most of our routine experiences disappear from memory almost immediately. If you are anything like me, you get in the car, drive somewhere you’ve been a thousand times before, pull up, get out, and suddenly realise you barely even remember the journey itself. You obviously drove, stopped at traffic lights and avoided crashing into things, but because your brain already knew the pattern, most of the drive happened on complete autopilot… and it’s even easier now I don’t have to change gears anymore. Thank fook for the automatic. Humans do this constantly. We predict things, filter things and automate familiar experiences because if we had to consciously process every tiny detail of every moment of every day we would mentally collapse before our cheeky 11am coffee break. That’s why so many experiences we go through every single day become, well… forgettable. You expect the hotel room to be ready when you arrive. You expect somebody at reception to hand you a key, point you towards the lift or stairs and solve any mini problems in the quickest and most logical way possible, so when all of those things happen exactly as predicted, your brain simply processes the experience efficiently and moves on because nothing emotionally interesting actually happened. But when something interrupts that predictable pattern in a creative, emotional or unexpected way, your brain suddenly pays far more attention because it wasn’t expecting it. That’s why the Joshie story mattered so freaking much. The family expected the hotel to find the giraffe and simply post it back. Problem solved. No dramas here people. Everybody moves on with their lives. But instead, the hotel staff created this ridiculously brilliant, fake holiday for the giraffe that made it feel like Joshie was genuinely out there living his best life in the California sun and making mates along the way. They went to completely unreasonable measures just to bring a little bit of joy to a child and back up his dad’s white lie, and that exact unpredictability is what made the whole thing unforgettable. Humans remember meaningful and surprising moments far more than they remember predictable and functional ones. The hotel didn’t just solve the problem. They transformed a completely ordinary customer service interaction into a story that people are still retelling years later… and I think that’s the bit most of us miss as business owners. People rarely remember what was efficient, but they almost always remember how something made them feel. I mean, I almost bloody cried the first time I read the Joshie story because I instantly thought about how my own son would feel seeing his favourite toy off living its best life and making mates on holiday. I take Lightning McQueen with me on work trips because I miss my son Rocco, and I take silly little photos of him at random places because I know my son lights up when he sees them. He genuinely thinks daddy and Lightning are away together having a good time, so this little giraffe story hit a proper emotional note for me. The Joshie story stopped being “good customer service” and instantly became something far more human because you could feel the love, effort and humanity inside the decision those hotel staff made… and that kind of creativity can never be automated. Nor bloody should it. I hope this story sparks the creativity inside you to go against the grain when you can. To be unpredictable with your kindness and to find ways to connect with others that might be out of the ordinary. People remember people who thought about them in different and unique ways. I think, over the coming years, businesses and brands will increasingly be judged on what they choose to keep human. Automate the predictable. Humanise the meaningful. Love ya. James - The People’s Branding Mentor

title: #305 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 2)
description: nas edições anteriores #303 | Marcas multiespécie #304 | Offline é o novo hype (parte 1) tempo de leitura: 4 minutos para entender 💡 Passamos os últimos dois anos falando, desejando, criando, repetindo o termo “offline” nos nossos planos de mídia e carrosseis de Instagram, a ponto dele ter se tornado também um grande hype . Por um lado, pessoas performando atividades online apenas para postar. Por outro, marcas usando esse movimento como desculpa pra poluir visualmente o mundo real ou encher as nossas casas de objetos desnecessários. (Nem tudo deveria ter um anúncio. O mundo não precisa de mais um brinde com o seu logo sem intenção nenhuma). E agora? _ Este não é um manifesto anti-offline. De maneira alguma. A gente não deve desistir de materializar as nossas marcas ou criar experiências no mundo real (não vamos desistir) . Mas neste processo, é importante entender duas coisas: 1. “Offline é o novo luxo” é uma maneira muito simplista de olhar para essa tendência. Ela é indiscutivelmente atrativa para as marcas de luxo, que sempre pautaram a sua comunicação na estética e estilos de vida capazes de diferenciar as pessoas. Quando a estética “comum” é cronicamente online, feita por IA e vidrada em uma tela, o luxo busca ilustrações feitas à mão e experiências sensoriais. Mas a necessidade de desconectar vai além da performance e da distinção social. O que torna o “offline” um movimento muito maior que qualquer trend é justamente a sua capacidade de resgatar uma série de aspectos que têm se perdido na vida moderna. A presença, a atenção, o processo, o aprendizado, a conexão com outras pessoas, a dificuldade (e, consequentemente, a resiliência)… E as tantas sensações, rituais e habilidades que só o mundo real proporciona. Objetos físicos, eventos e atividades manuais devem seguir parte da estratégia das marcas. Não para gerar percepção de luxo ou para fazer igual a uma ou outra. Muito menos para criar novos espaços de mídia que “chamam mais atenção”. E sim pela sua capacidade de interromper o scroll infinito, de ser um lembrete da vida que acontece fora das telas, de gerar valor e, quem sabe, até transformação real nas pessoas. O que nos leva ao segundo ponto. _ 2. Quando o offline se torna hype, é preciso fugir do lugar comum Em 2025, fizemos a primeira edição de uma revista impressa. Ela foi a realização de um sonho antigo, e a materialização da Bits to Brands em cores, ilustrações e páginas enviadas para todo o Brasil. Seu projeto editorial foi feito em outubro de 2024, e a sua impressão em dezembro. Na época, as revistas já começavam a despontar como símbolo de nostalgia - mas não dava para imaginar que seria um movimento tão intenso. Desde então, diversas marcas imprimiram revistas - e serviram café, receberam clubes do livro, ofereceram corridas de rua, distribuíram bonés bordados, estamparam câmeras analógicas… Assim, apenas na sua segunda edição, uma revista não é mais surpreendente ou inovadora. Do mesmo jeito que, em 2026, um boné também não é. (Aliás, um boné vira parte de uma coleção que está chegando a 20 unidades por aqui) O valor do offline não vai a lugar nenhum, mas fazer o básico não é mais o suficiente. O desafio é seguir se reinventando no mesmo formato. A boa notícia é que aí mora a diversão. Porque na tentativa de despertar o que há de mais humano em alguém (a presença, o contato, a memória), precisamos ser humanos primeiro . (criativos, sensíveis, curiosos). Fazer mais ou menos do mesmo jeito, mas um pouco diferente. Fazer mais ou menos a mesma coisa, mas fazer também algo novo. Tornar algo uma tradição, investir de fato em um ritual de marca - mas buscar novas formas de encontrar prazer no processo, e encantar as pessoas com o resultado. Uma revista, a gente já tinha feito. Um álbum de figurinhas foi a primeira vez. Vida longa à nossa imaginação e capacidade de reinvenção - bem humanas, e bem brasileiras :) _ A segunda edição da Revista Bits to Brands está no ar. Neste momento, ela está sendo presenteada para clientes e parceiros da Bits. Mas você vai poder garantir a sua. Na próxima edição da newsletter, dia 15/09, traremos todos os detalhes - e o link! Fiquem de olho porque a quantidade é limitada. Até lá, todos os detalhes estão sendo revelados aos poucos no nosso Instagram. :) para continuar a conversa nas redes sociais e convidar mais gente para cá, compartilhe usando o botão abaixo ou marcando a @bitstobrands Share para inspirar ✨ Essa campanha da Hermann Miller é um ótimo exemplo de como transformar um benefício funcional em conceito criativo. Porque uma cadeira de escritório não precisa querer salvar o mundo ou te fazer chorar com um anúncio. Ela é feita para você sentar melhor. E essa mensagem, com a execução certa, fica irresistível. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 O primeiro fim de semana do Rock in Rio foi marcado pela chuva - e pelas filas para pegar brindes nas ativações das marcas. Até agora, destacamos: O karaokê gigante do Itaú (por criar uma experiência memorável verdadeiramente integrada ao evento) A collab entre Uber e LATAM (por entenderem que, juntas, elas poderiam chamar mais atenção do que separadas) _ Para ficar de olho: hoje acontece o primeiro evento da Apple com o novo CEO , John Ternus, no comando. Primeiro, é preciso acertar a estratégia do negócio e, a partir dela, garantir que exista uma estratégia de marca capaz de viabilizá-la”. para mais conteúdo 📚 🖼️ siga a Bits no Instagram [link] 📚 confira uma seleção de livros na nossa biblioteca [link] 🎧 ouça o podcast Tudo que Importa [link] 🤝 anuncie na Bits - peça o nosso mídia kit em contato@bitstobrands.com 📩 assine essa newsletter , caso não tenha recebido por e-mail :) Subscribe now para dar um tchau 👋🏼 Nestes dois textos, quis dividir com vocês um pouco de todas as reflexões do último ano, que resultaram em uma revista impressa com álbum de figurinhas, e também uma nova palestra. Acredito no físico, no impresso e no analógico para muito além da trend ou do potencial de chamar atenção. Acredito tanto que, antes de falar, eu faço. E é fazendo - à mão, com calma, com muita troca e com todo o talento e entusiasmo de todos os envolvidos - que eu percebo o quanto isso tem valor. Um valor que não vai a lugar nenhum. description: nas edições anteriores #302 | Os oráculos da timeline #303 | Marcas multiespécie tempo de leitura: 5 minutos para entender 💡 Já vai fazer dois anos que a expressão “o offline é o novo luxo” se disseminou pela internet. Ora como análise de tendência, ora como sinalização de virtude. Nós também somos um pouco culpados disso: Em janeiro de 2025, prestes a lançar a primeira edição da nossa revista impressa, estávamos mergulhados no “offline”. E não só a gente. Foi um verão em que muita gente procurou desconectar, e assim seguiu pelas estações. De câmeras analógicas a aulas de cerâmica, palavras cruzadas, telefones fixos… Todo tipo de estratégia (e produto) foi surgindo para ajudar. Começando, inclusive, pelas marcas de luxo. Porque não é uma coincidência que este seja o adjetivo mais utilizado ao lado da palavra “offline”. Tanto porque o “luxo” é mais valioso e raro, quanto porque ele é aquilo que foge do comum. Quando uma estética ou comportamento se torna o básico, aquilo que todo mundo tem, beirando até o “brega” - performar superioridade intelectual e social é se afastar dela. (A relação entre consumo e performance social está super bem explicada em Coisa de Rico , de Michel Alcoforado). Se nos últimos anos o comum é ser hiperconectado, cronicamente online e passar incontáveis horas arrastando para cima imóvel, o que passa a comunicar luxo e status é desconectar. Ler livros de verdade, fazer atividade física ao ar livre, acessórios tecnológicos mais vintage, encontros para discutir temas específicos, o resgate dos hábitos e atividades sociais das avós (do tricô ao nonna-maxxing )… É por essas e outras que a Miu Miu tem um clube do livro, a Bottega Veneta lançou um jogo de Jenga, a Prada fez uma floricultura e as marcas de luxo têm disputado espaço para fazer ativações nos grandes torneios de tênis pelo mundo. O offline se tornou, sim, sinônimo de luxo. Mas não pára por aí. _ O offline se tornou território de desejo das marcas por motivos certos e errados, racionais e abstratos, mas muitos deles ancorados em comportamentos e demandas bem reais. Um deles é a distinção social. Mas ativações no mundo real, eventos, experiências e objetos físicos despertam interesse também porque são comunitários, sensoriais, duráveis, memoráveis e humanos. Cada um desses aspectos parte de demandas da vida contemporânea que começam no excesso de telas, mas se estendem para a ausência de interações sociais, a substituição do corpo físico pela imagem editada de alguém e até o tal “AI Slop”. Num parque a gente não precisa ficar se perguntando se algo é IA ou não a cada dois minutos (ainda). Porque o offline é comunidade , ele nos permite lembrar que não estamos sozinhos nos nossos gostos e hobbies - seja correr uma meia maratona, seja ter sido fã da Xuxa na infância. Porque o offline é sensorial , ele nos lembra que cada um é um corpo, e não apenas um cérebro e as pontas dos dedos. E que um corpo é capaz de sentir gostos, cheiros, toques, de dançar, cantar, esbarrar, ver e ser visto e se relacionar - de verdade. Porque o offline é durável , ele se torna representação no mundo real de quem a gente é. Aquilo que decora os nossos ambientes, que compõe as nossas coleções , que está pendurado nas nossas bolsas e mochilas ou até geladeiras - ajuda a contar a nossa história. Diga-me o que colecionas e te direi quem és. Porque o offline é memorável, ele é uma grande oportunidade para as marcas investirem seus orçamentos de comunicação de forma mais assertiva. Estamos descobrindo que reunir um grupo de pessoas verdadeiramente atentas e interessadas tem mais valor do que atingir milhões de views sabe-se lá de quem. E porque o offline é humano, ele é o único ambiente onde a gente vivencia o tempo de forma linear, a arte de forma artesanal e o mundo conforme a nossa própria curadoria de experiências - e não a de um algortimo. Não é à toa que todo mundo quer mais disso. _ Passamos os últimos dois anos falando, desejando, criando, repetindo o termo “offline” nos nossos planos de mídia e carrosseis de Instagram, a ponto dele ter se tornado também um grande hype . Por um lado, pessoas performando atividades online apenas para postar. Por outro, marcas usando esse movimento como desculpa pra poluir visualmente o mundo real ou encher as nossas casas de objetos desnecessários. (Nem tudo deveria ter um anúncio. O mundo não precisa de mais um brinde com o seu logo sem intenção nenhuma). Uma editoria no Instagram para explorar marcas brasileiras de diferentes regiões e segmentos, e tudo que elas têm a nos ensinar. Já passamos por Tramontina , Xeque Mate e Turma da Mônica . E se você tiver sugestões, pode deixar aqui nos comentários. para fazer parte da conversa 💬 O Instagram atualizou a sua tipografia e todo o seu universo visual . E é claro que todo mundo queria ter uma opinião. title: The Personal Brand Trap: Why Humans Shouldn’t Think of Themselves as Brands
description: When I was a wee little boy growing up, I wanted to be a fireman. It seemed considerably more achievable than becoming a ThunderCat or Batman, which were my other career choices when I was eight. At school I had absolutely no clue what I wanted to do as a career. Potentially something arty or sporty, but back in the 90s I was told neither of those were money-makers, so I had to think about getting a proper job. Today, I would classify myself as a designer and educator helping the next generation of creatives build more opportunity for themselves. That feels very aligned with who I am today. But I have also been a barman, factory worker, waiter, tattoo apprentice, window cleaner, failed businessman, unemployable bum, and many other things on the journey to finding this particular version of me. And that is one of the wonderful things about being a human… nobody really freaking knows who they’re going to become. The person you are today is probably very different from the person you were five years ago, and if you’re doing this thing called life properly, there’s a good chance the person you’ll become five years from now will look different again. And, from what my mum tells me… that’s completely normal. Most of us are making it up as we go, collecting experiences and continuously falling forward into newer versions of ourselves… we’re supposed to evolve. So in this little article I want to share my perspective on a topic that I think deserves a little more questioning: personal branding. More specifically, I want to explore why I don’t think humans should think of themselves as brands, and why applying brand logic to a human being can potentially do more harm than good. Thanks for reading The Real Brand Life! Subscribe for free to receive new posts. Now, I’m not here to suggest that personal branding doesn’t exist. That would cause a riot. Instead, I’d like to challenge some of the advice being peddled around willy-nilly on the dopamine drug train that is social media. To do that, I think we first need to agree on the difference between brand logic and human logic. A brand’s job is to reduce complexity. Brands are trying to be recognised at scale and for that to happen, they need to simplify things. They need to make themselves easier to understand, remember and choose. They do that better when they are associated with a couple of very clear ideas. Humans, on the other hand, operate very differently my friends. We change our minds all the freaking time. We become interested in new things. We learn stuff, we grow our minds and then we see the world differently because of it. And an important thing to add is that humans don’t naturally operate at scale. We evolved in small communities and tribes, not in front of thousands of random people online. So if brands become stronger through consistency and humans become stronger through change, are we really sure those two things belong together? That’s why I find phrases like “you are your brand” and “everyone has a personal brand” a little, well… problematic. Being known for something and being a brand are not the same thing. I understand that these phrases are often being used as shortcuts, but even when I account for that nuance, I still think they fundamentally misunderstand what a brand is… and what a human needs. Now, I don’t want this to come across as a rant or a black-and-white argument, as some of the advice coming out of the personal brand camp is incredibly useful. Visibility matters for sure because if nobody knows what the heck you do, how on earth are they supposed to hire you? Other people need to know you exist people. I absolutely believe humans should become known. Known for doing good work, having interesting ideas, standing for something and making a positive impact on the people around them. But becoming known and becoming a product are not the same thing. Being known, or what most would simply call a reputation, is something people gift you over time. It forms through your behaviour and the way you consistently show up for yourself. You don’t have to manufacture it, force it or spend every waking minute trying to manage how you’re perceived by others. A reputation happens naturally as you continue growing into the person you’re becoming. And this is where I think we can run into trouble because the moment we start thinking of ourselves as a brand, our focus can shift. Instead of asking, “Who am I becoming?” we start asking, “How will this look to other people?” The danger is that we start viewing ourselves through the eyes of an audience before we’ve had chance to fully understand ourselves… we start looking at ourselves from the outside in. At first, that might not sound like too much of a problem. In fact, it actually sounds pretty bloody sensible. If you’re running a business, surely you should care about how people feel when they see you. But I don’t believe growth and perception always want the same thing. The thing about growth is that it can look a bit messy from the outside. You change your mind, let go of old ideas and, more often than we’d like to admit, realise you got something wrong. That’s all part of the process. And brand logic doesn’t particularly reward that kind of thinking. Brands gain strength through their consistency. They keep showing up in roughly the same way until people know exactly what to expect from them. And I think that’s where a lot of people can run into a bit of an issue. The more successful a personal brand becomes, the more pressure there can be to keep being the person your audience already knows. To keep talking about the same things, showing up in the same way and feeding the machine that made people pay attention in the first place. That’s the personal brand trap. The human becomes responsible for holding onto a version of themselves they may have already outgrown. And as we see more people choosing freelance careers, building solo businesses and creating opportunities for themselves online, I think this becomes an increasingly important conversation to navigate. I know that perception matters, visibility matters, being known matters, and creating opportunity matters… but so does growth as a human being. Perhaps the challenge isn’t figuring out how to turn people into brands… instead it’s figuring out how to help people become known without trapping them. I’d hate to think that personal branding, the very thing so many people turn to in search of more opportunity, could end up becoming the thing that stops them from becoming who they’re supposed to be. So if I can leave you with a little bit of advice here it would be this: focus on the things you want to be known for, but don’t lose sight of the person you’re becoming along the way. Maybe the goal isn’t to manage perception at all. Perhaps it’s simply to become someone worth paying attention to. Humans are supposed to evolve. Brands are supposed to repeat. The problems arise when we start applying the rules of one to the other, so don’t flatten yourself into a product mindset just because the internet tells you that’s the secret to success. Focus on becoming known for your craft, your kindness and your character. Keep sharing what matters to you because opportunity has a funny way of finding people who do. Just please remember to sprinkle a little patience on yourself along the way. Your mate, James Thoughts on this? Comment below team. I’m excited to hear what you think. title: Tiny moments that become a real brand.
description: Before we jump into this week’s article, reminder that my new book No Bullsh*t Branding is available for pre-order… and if you pre-order by the end of today (Sunday 31st May) you get a bonus freebie bundle, including the Book Club, the new MVB Course, limited edition MBJ merch, and digital downloads. Check it out here ! Thank you all so much for your support. Last weekend the weather was delicious. So delicious that myself, Kate and Rocco went to the beach for the day to hang with our friends (Jamie & Mel) and their little kiddos… it was one of those beautiful little days that will live long in the memory bank. We were down at West Wittering beach near Chichester. It’s this big, magical stretch of sand where, when the tide goes out, the beach becomes absolutely colossal. Perfect for kids because there’s endless space to run around and play… it becomes the worlds largest, sandy adventure space. Scattered across the beach are these little pools of warm water left behind by the retreating tide… tiny, stinky lakes full of seaweed, shells, wet sand and mess. Basically heaven for a little dude like Rocco. And he was more than happy exploring them completely alone while the rest of his friends sat further up the beach eating lunch and digging holes. He was so happy, so I wanted him to just ‘be’… so I stayed and watched. After maybe an hour of watching him play in the same giant puddle, I eventually wandered up to him and asked him to come back to “base camp” so we could put more suncream on, tag mummy back in and potentially allow me to eat some lunch. But he was having absolutely none of it. Everything I offered was ignored. Every negotiation tactic I’d learned in business was useless, and every attempt to reason with him about how the sun was really hot and he needed protecting from it was completely pointless. Eventually Kate, my wonderful wife, spotted my slow descent into parental defeat from afar and wandered over with all the supplies we needed. And at that point, I just accepted reality and decided to play the waiting game until he was ready to move on himself… I mean, the sun would go down eventually, I was sure of that, and I also now had a sandwich. But there was a lesson hiding inside all of this. When you have very little to negotiate with, the situation you are in becomes incredibly difficult to win… and this got me thinking about the very beginning of my own business journey. It was so difficult to find any money-making opportunities when I started because I had so little to negotiate with. No Leverage. I had no real portfolio, no website, no testimonials and, in absolute honesty… very little knowledge. I wouldn’t have hired me. As you know, for me, a brand is a recognisable reputation, and at that point I was neither recognised nor did I really have a reputation worth knowing… unless it was “having a good time down the pub” - I was real good at that. And this got me thinking about all the newbies entering the world right now. All the junior creatives trying to find work and carve out a place for themselves while also navigating challenges I never had to deal with. Things like social media pressure, constant comparison, AI, tech and the heavy, heavy, heavy psychological weight of feeling like you need to live your life so publicly online. Now, I’m not saying my era had it easy at all… every generation has its own struggles. But I do think it’s harder now than it was 20 years ago, mainly for the reasons I mentioned above. So I want to try an answer this question today. How do we build a business when, right at the beginning, we have nothing to be recognised for and no reputation backing us up? So… lets chat. Yes, you might not have the clients yet. You might not have the case studies, the swanky portfolio, the testimonials or the years of industry proof backing up your ambition. But what you do have is YOU. That matters far more than many people think. Because there are already so many things you are recognised for outside of your “business circles”. Your attitude, your energy, your humour, your kindness, your curiosity, your willingness to help, your ability to make people feel good around you, your ability to stay optimistic when everything feels difficult or half empty. What I’m trying to suggest here is that even if you do not yet have a recognisable reputation around your work, you already have years and years of building a recognisable reputation around your humanness and character, and that is a beautifully fun place to start… that becomes your negotiating power. One of the huge advantages early stage creatives have is that they are not yet boxed in by the “rules” of the industry. They are not trapped by client expectations or weighed down by years of process refinement and predictability. They still have “all the raws”… raw energy, raw enthusiasm and raw creativity to boot. In the beginning, it’s often your willingness to care about others and build relationships that sparks the most opportunity. Helping a mate out for freebies, offering your services to friends of friends in exchange for tickets to their latest gig… that scrappy little world of free crafty goodness is where most of us cut our teeth in the industry. When I was starting out, I bartered constantly. I used my skills to build experience, and the more experience I gained, the more confidence I built. In return, I’d get free coffee, free jewellery, free food, whilst also building relationships with local humans… whatever people could offer at the time instead of money, I said yes to. Looking back, I actually think there’s something incredibly beautiful about that stage of the journey. I mean, bartering is how worlds were built. When you’re starting out, you still have permission to try almost anything you can to keep the lights on and keep the dream alive. You can knock on doors, start conversations, help people, make things, experiment, build fabulous little ditties and push your creativity out into the world. And over time, people begin recognising you for those behaviours. For your energy, your effort, your generosity, your consistency and the way you make people feel. Almost without noticing it, those tiny moments become the foundations of a recognisable reputation. A real brand. So if you are at the beginning, listening to a noisy world telling you that “designers are fucked” or “the creative industry is doomed,” remember that most of it is just distraction… like a lot of news on the inter webs. Don’t fall into the trap of blindly listening to these people. Many of them have their own agenda too… which is often making sure they stay relevant and irreplaceable in a changing world. Instead, use your creativity and your energy to build relationships. Make cool stuff and send it to people. Write a little hand-drawn note thanking somebody for inspiring you. Instead of sending the same PDF portfolio to 400 people like everybody else is doing, start more real, human conversations. Barter your services. Collaborate with people. Send a hand written letter. Deliver someone a little product with your work on it. Go above and beyond simply because you care enough to do so. Become recognised for how much effort you are putting in… that is a reputation that opportunities will eventually flow towards. Stay Focused, Stay Crafty… Your creativity is your super duper power. James - The Peoples Branding Mentor

Check it out ! “ coincidence ,” by K Bahr on Flickr “A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed.“ Dear friend of TAoN Suzanne M sent me a link the other day to a deep-dive article about coincidences . I’d never given this subject much thought, but it turned out to be pretty interesting. And as Suzanne detected, there was a noticing/attention angle that I couldn’t help dwelling on. A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed. If I walk past a childhood friend I haven’t seen in 20 years in some airport where neither of us lives, one of us has to notice the other for the coincidence to “count,” as it were. In some ways, “ the amazing thing is not that these things occur, it’s that we notice them, ” according to David Spiegelhalter, a professor at the University of Cambridge who studies such things, as quoted in Julie Beck’s’ Atlantic article. You could say that being more attentive leads to registering more coincidences. Spiegelhalter, the article notes, has a website where people can submit their coincidence experiences, and claims to have collected something like 5,000 of them. The most common form is “ finding a link with someone you meet .” Obviously, this suggests that people who are looking for connections — who are open, curious, attentive to others — are more likely to find unexpected ones. “Coincidences never happen to me at all, because I never notice anything,” Spiegelhalter says (somewhat jokingly). “I never talk to anybody on trains. If I’m with a stranger, I don’t try to find a connection with them … .” I admit it never really occurred to me that there could be coincidence-friendly types . But Beck also cites another researcher who has found that certain personality traits are linked to experiencing more coincidences—people who describe themselves as religious or spiritual, people who are self-referential (or likely to relate information from the external world back to themselves), and people who are high in meaning-seeking are all coincidence-prone. The article goes on to explore everything from Jung’s idea of synchronicity to popular notions of the paranormal. Possibly the opposite of missing coincidences is reading too much meaning into mere chance occurrences that look like something more. The world shapes our attention, but sometimes attention shapes our world — for better or worse! That said, I’m attracted to this idea that “finding a link with someone you meet” is the most-reported form of coincidence. It’s a nice frame for chatting with someone new: Be curious, be open — and look for a happy coincidence or two. Leave a comment Thank you Suzanne! Noticing is about other people, too. title: Wild, As In Harmonious
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for September is STRIPES. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . So many great contributions! Check it out ! “You need to go out into the world and look.” If you pay attention to the idea of paying attention, you have no doubt encountered the words of Mary Oliver, from her poems, essays, interviews. Oliver attracted fans ranging from John Waters to Oprah, from Stephen Colbert to Lucy Dacus. In The Art of Noticing book, I quoted from her poem “ Sometimes ”: Instructions for living a life: Pay attention. Be astonished. Tell about it. But the truth is, I didn’t really know much about Oliver’s life, and even my familiarity with her work was pretty thin. So I was very excited to see the new documentary about her, Mary Oliver: Saved By the Beauty of the World, via the PBS series American Masters. You can watch on the PBS site , or on YouTube . I recommend it! The documentary covers Oliver’s career as well her personal life, traumas included. (The title borrows from her line: “I got saved by poetry, and I got saved by the beauty of the world.”) I won’t attempt to summarize the whole thing, but I’ll share some of of the TAoN- relevant highlights. Oliver grew up in Ohio, an outsider drawn mostly to the natural world and “dead poets.” She preferred noticing to being noticed. Later, in her 20s, she learned from the intensity with which her partner, photographer Molly Malone Cook, interacted with others. Another of her familiar quotations: “ Attention without feeling … is only a report. ” Oliver and Cook lived in Provincetown, where Oliver continued her practice, attentive and poetic, walking the same paths to discover what she missed before. In time, she won major awards, and a significant audience, but to some extent the literary establishment pigeonholed her as someone who basically just went for walks and wrote about it. One person in the documentary calls her an icon of the hermit life. But that’s not the whole story. “You need to go out into the world and look,” the poet Mark Doty says in the documentary, and that’s exactly what Oliver was doing — even if it was in the nearby woods. Her appreciation of the natural world was no retreat. It was the opposite. “ Attention is the beginning of devotion, ” as she (famously) wrote in the title essay of her collection Upstream . This is perhaps her central lesson for those of us who care to go out into the world land look. “You can get ecstatic over a box of matches,” she remarks in one interview clip. And in other she makes the point I love the most: “If you love something, you give it a lot of attention. And if you give something a lot of attention, you very often learn to love it.” Yet another widely quoted Oliver line is her poetic question : “ what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life? ” Her own life might not sound “wild” in the way we commonly use that word. But if you don’t have time for the whole documentary, check out the clip below discussing her poem “ Wild Geese ” — and ultimately pointing out that wild can also mean natural, harmonious. The Economy Is the Medium: The Market Seth Goldstein, July 2026 In the summer of 2022 the most alive room in digital art was a minting floor. Bright Moments, the gallery I founded, had built its whole model on a single inversion: the moment a generative artwork comes into existence (the transaction itself) could be an event you attend. Minting live onchain wasn’t new. Art Blocks had made the long-distance reveal a genre. Bright Moments’ invention was staging the mint in person: a room watching the transaction become the work. The CryptoVenetians in Venice Beach in 2021, a thousand tokens generated one at a time in front of the people who claimed them, were the proof. You stood in a room in Venice Beach or Manhattan; your city’s token was generated in front of you, and the market was the evening’s program. We were minting our way around the world, city by city. That July we were in London for Proof of People week at 18 Albemarle Street. The European chapter begins there: we brought the European artists over to mint their CryptoLondoners in person (Zancan, Ciphrd from fxhash, Andreas Gysin, Kim himself). That week is when I first met Ganbrood. They came to see what a live mint felt like. That is also where I met Kim Asendorf. The first thing that ever passed between us was, fittingly, a provenance problem ... Baby, I Love You Derek Simpson, August 2026 Whenever we hear “Baby” invoked, imagine the seer is addressing this Spirit as it is revealed in the singular form of another human being. In the presence of a lover, a friend, or even a complete stranger, the seer catches a glimpse of Baby , flickering like a flame inside Her human conduit. Taking this momentary incarnation, Baby connects the seer back to something essential: a deep well of omnipresent love that lies within. This vision, and the epiphany it presents, arouse a sudden rush of passion within the seer, a moment of OH preceding either a hysterical fit or the direct channeling of a Rock ‘n’ Roll incantation. Each of Baby ’s adopted forms provides its own unique connection back to loving awareness, so Rock ‘n’ Roll has embraced a wide range of alternate titles for Baby . When Darling or Dearest are used, along with the title Baby itself, the seer is addressing one of Spirit’s many androgynous forms ... Art Which Can’t Be Art Alan Kaprow, July 2026 When I speak of activities and contexts that don’t suggest art, I don’t mean that an event like brushing my teeth each morning is chosen and then set into a conventional art context, as Duchamp and many others since him have done. That strategy, by which an art-identifying frame (such as a gallery or theater) confers “art value” or “art discourse” on some nonart object, idea, or event, was, in Duchamp’s initial move, sharply ironic. It forced into confrontation a whole bundle of sacred assumptions about creativity, professional skill, individuality, spirituality, modernism, and the presumed value and function of high art itself. But later it became trivialized, as more and more nonart was put on exhibit by other artists. Regardless of the merits of each case, the same truism was headlined every time we saw a stack of industrial products in a gallery, every time daily life was enacted on a stage: that anything can be estheticized, given the right art packages to put it into. But why should we want to estheticize “anything”? All the irony was lost in those presentations, the provocative questions forgotten. To go on making this kind of move in art seemed to me unproductive ... Where Reality Renders Molly Hankins, July 2026 If we imagine all of our individual perspectives as filaments of consciousness, or light as Kabbalah describes it, we can theorize a place where all of those filaments meet. It is at this convergence point where reality is assembled and ultimately perceived. As described by Peruvian-born anthropologist and author Carlos Castaneda, who wrote a series of books based on the teachings of a Yaqui shaman named Don Juan Matus, this “assemblage point” is where individual consciousness merges into collective awareness to create reality. As we become aware of and intentional in how we program our filaments, we learn to reshape reality, which is the Great Work of Yaqui shamans, as well as alchemists and Hermeticists. In the early 1960s Castaneda became an apprentice to Don Juan, who he claimed could manipulate time and space, and began exploring psychedelic plant medicine under his supervision. These experiences brought Castaneda into what he called “non-ordinary reality,” and from there he was able to explore consciousness beyond the boundaries of ordinary perception. From this vantage point, Don Juan was able to show Castaneda how much power our perception has to influence both our lives and the whole of humanity ... Tetragrammaton on Grünewald As the Renaissance entered its height across Europe, the mysterious German painter Matthias Grünewald looked backwards. Rejecting the classicism of the day, he committed himself to the style of medieval painting that had dominated Northern Europe before Italy’s influence. Gothic works laden with fantastic colours and strange perspectival choices, his paintings are as much about the spiritual as they are the religious The supernatural colours that emanate from Christ’s body, and from the jewel like on his hands and feet, emphasise the power of his divinity, creating in the viewer not a sense of understanding but one of awe ... title: What is "the gravity of average" and why is it holding you back?
description: I grew up believing one thing: Don’t be average. Looking back now, as an older, slightly fatter man, there’s something wonderfully ironic about that particular piece of advice. While every person in authority was telling me not to become average, the systems around me were teaching me exactly how to become it. School teaches us there was one right answer. Business teaches us there’s a right process. Algorithms tell us there’s a right format. Most industries have their own best practices, and society at large constantly reminds us that fitting in is safer than standing out. None of these proven systems are bad. In fact, they’re incredibly useful. They help us educate millions of little people, build reliable businesses, and make sense of an increasingly complicated world. But when you start stacking them on top of one another, year after year, decade after decade… something intriguing happens. They all pull us in the exact same direction: Toward what’s proven Toward what’s predictable Toward what’s familiar Toward the flipping middle We hear a lot these days about falling test scores, declining creativity, and a lack of ambition. I’m not convinced that’s the whole story. I think we’re living inside an ecosystem of invisible forces that constantly reward the safest path. Millions of perfectly sensible decisions, made by perfectly sensible people, combine to suck us toward the same ideas until we all end up in the exact same place… the fookin’ middle. I call this: the gravity of average. Whether we realize it or not, we’ve been caught in its invisible pull since the day we were born… damn it. Here are the five layers of gravity conspiring against us all, and why you need to fight them with everything you’ve got to protect your individual magic. 1. Educational gravity Our first experience of this gravity starts in the classroom. School has an incredibly difficult job: educating millions of children fairly and consistently, often with limited resources and enormous expectations. The only way to make that possible is to rely on standardized curricula, rigid grading schemes, and easily measured outcomes. From a very young age, we learn to optimize for what gets rewarded … the gold stars, the praise from teachers, the good-old pats on the back. Before long, we’re no longer just learning the subject, we’re learning how to succeed within the system. The educational environment doesn’t intentionally produce average people. Far from it. But when success is measured in the exact same way for everyone, it’s only natural that millions of children begin chasing the exact same things. The more people optimize for the identical outcome, the more they will eventually look alike… it’s the logical outcome of a predictable system. 2. Economic gravity Businesses only exist if they survive, and to do that, they have to make rational decisions. If a pricing model has worked before, why change it? If a marketing strategy has proven successful, why reinvent it? If a competitor is growing using a particular approach, it’s only natural to copy it. None of these are bad decisions. Economist Harold Hotelling described this exact phenomenon in what became known as Hotelling’s Law . When businesses compete for the same customers, they naturally drift toward one another rather than away. Differentiation feels risky, while similarity feels sensible. Over time, this way of thinking compounds. What starts as “best practice” gradually becomes the default way of doing business. When an entire industry chases the identical measures of success (revenue, profit, or market share), even the most original business ideas eventually drift toward the average when they optimize for the same thing. 3. Social gravity As humans, we’ve always worried about belonging. For most of human history, being accepted by the group dramatically increased our chances of not becoming dead. That instinct is still hardwired into us. One of my favourite psychology experiments that backs this up comes from Solomon Asch . Participants were invited into a room to complete what they thought was a simple test about the length of a few lines. What they didn’t know was that everyone else in the room was an actor hired to be in on the experiment. The answers were obvious, but one by one, the actors deliberately gave the wrong answer. Faced with an entire room disagreeing with them, many participants ignored what they could clearly see and went along with the crowd instead. Around 75% of people conformed at least once, even though the group was clearly wrong. Nobody has to tell us to fit in. We just learn which parts of ourselves earn acceptance and which parts are safer left hidden. 4. Algorithmic gravity Welcome to the newest kid on the block. Algorithms don’t care about “silly” things like originality… all they give a poop about is retention. The easiest way to predict what will keep your attention is to look at what has already worked. Successful ideas become recommendations. Recommendations become trends. Trends become the templates that every influencer and their dog starts copying. Before long, thousands of people are creating different versions of the exact same thing because that’s what the system keeps serving up. Social media isn’t in the business of finding the next brilliant idea. It’s in the business of keeping us scrolling, and scrolling, and scrolling. And the easiest way to do that is by feeding us a slightly repackaged version of the average… the baseline of everything the system has already gobbled up before. 5. Professional gravity Every profession develops its own “playbook.” Designers have processes, marketers have foolproof plans, and consultants have their frameworks. Most of these defaults exist because someone, at some point, solved a real problem for a real person… hurrah. The danger happens when best practice subtly becomes the only practice. The longer an approach survives unquestioned, the more it feels like common sense. Before long, entire industries are repeating formulas that worked 30 years ago, even though the world has completely evolved around them. The comfort zone is a very dangerous place. Nothing grows there, as they say. The optimization trap What I’ve realized about these five forces is that they all share the exact same mischievous mechanism. Every system must decide what success looks like and, once it does, the rest of us naturally optimize for it. School rewards grades. Business rewards revenue. Algorithms reward engagement. Society rewards acceptance. Professions reward best practice. None of the above are bad… but when millions of people chase the exact same measures of success, gravity takes over. Human beings are remarkably good at adapting to their environment. The more we align ourselves with the same definition of success, the more we begin to resemble one another. And today, more people than ever are finding themselves in the middle. For most of history, becoming competent at something took years of deliberate practice. Today, technology can get almost anyone to “good enough” in a matter of minutes. Technology is closing the gap from below, while optimization is closing the gap from above. People who once struggled to produce competent work can now create something perfectly passable with better tools. At the same time, many of the people who were once exceptional are handing more of their thinking over to those same tools. In the pursuit of speed they often sacrifice the originality and personality that made them stand out in the first place. One force lifts people into the middle. The other pulls people back towards it. Now, there is absolutely nothing wrong with being average. Millions of people build fulfilling careers, do meaningful work, and live brilliant lives without ever trying to stand out. But commercially, today, average is becoming a far riskier place to build a future. To riff on something Rory Sutherland once said: when you become logical, you become predictable. And when you become predictable, you become replaceable. That doesn’t mean you should reject logic or stop using new technology. It simply means those things are no longer enough. They help you meet the standard, yes, but they’ll never make you the obvious choice. I’ve come to believe that opportunity doesn’t flow toward the middle. It flows toward recognizable differences that people trust. The gravity of average never disappears. You simply decide whether to drift with it… or spend your time pushing against it. Maybe that’s what Mr. Hotelling was trying to tell us all along. Test the edges. - James This article first appeared in my Fast Company column. You can check it out here .

E o momento, que parecia ideal para sua consolidação definitiva e ganho de credibilidade, teve efeito contrário. As marcas de bet se tornaram tóxicas para as transmissões que patrocinaram, atrapalhando a experiência dos espectadores e gerando antipatia a todos os envolvidos. O canal, o narrador, a marca, até os jogadores. E é além de entretenimento. 61% das apostas sugeridas pela CazéTV foram perdidas.
